extracted.intended_audience: academics, research-integrity professionals, research administrators, and readers interested in academic misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and interpreting survey-based estimates of academic misconduct (fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, etc.), including methodological strengths/weaknesses and the policy implications of reported rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication defined as making up data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report states 17.9% (± 6.1%) of academics surveyed reported having fabricated (entirely invented) research data. Interpret such self- or indirect-reports cautiously given methodological caveats (see UCT, sampling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification (definition)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a distinct category from fabrication; check how the survey phrased and distinguished these behaviours when interpreting prevalence estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics form misuse (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics form misuse described as cutting corners on disclosing all ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how narrowly/broadly this is defined in the instrument and whether respondents understood the behaviour the same way researchers intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference misuse (definition/behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference misuse defined as cherry-picking papers to support the argument; operationalised in the survey as 'Using references to support predetermined arguments rather than illuminate debate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the most frequently reported malpractice (38.1% ± 5.1%). When using such items, examine examples and disciplinary norms to judge whether responses indicate deliberate misconduct or contested practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship abuse (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship abuse defined as adding your name to a paper without merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the survey wording and contextual cues; authorship norms vary by field, so prevalence estimates should be contextualised by discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-plagiarism (behavioural definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-plagiarising operationalisedas publishing extracts from the same piece in more than one location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 36.0% (± 7.6%) reported self-plagiarising. The article notes some respondents did not view this as unethical but as efficient — interpret prevalence against community norms and policy definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of the Unmatched Count Technique (UCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: UCT involves assigning participants to control or treatment lists and estimating the prevalence of a sensitive behaviour as the difference in mean number of checked items between groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors acknowledge UCT 'has quite a wide margin of error.' Critics (e.g., Ferric Fang) warn about its uncertain reliability and large error; researchers should report margins, validate estimates against other methods, and be cautious about over-interpreting UCT-derived prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare UCT estimates with direct-question results
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct questions about misconduct sometimes produced much lower rates than the UCT method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present both UCT and direct-question findings, examine discrepancies, and avoid privileging the more sensational estimate without careful justification or triangulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size adequacy and margin of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The survey sample was 215 UK academics; critics point out this is 'relatively few respondents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small samples increase uncertainty—report confidence intervals, margins of error, and avoid strong prevalence claims from limited N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling method and self-selection bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey was emailed online and encouraged to be shared, allowing self-selection of the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distribution method can attract especially motivated respondents, biasing prevalence estimates. Explicitly discuss recruitment, incentives to respond, and how self-selection may inflate or distort rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality checks (duplicates and out-of-scope responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors found significant numbers of duplicate questionnaires and people responding from outside the UK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and report de-duplication, geographic eligibility checks, and other quality controls; exclude invalid responses or account for them in sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and demographic skew
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent demographics were skewed: 27% Arts & Humanities, 46% social sciences; average reported publication rate was one paper per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sample composition matches the target population (e.g., all UK academics or research-active scientists). If skewed, avoid extrapolating prevalence to the broader research community without weighting or qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of prevalence calculation (difference-in-means estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion engaged in a sensitive behaviour was calculated as the difference in the mean number of statements between control and treatment groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure appropriate statistical modelling for UCT data, provide standard errors/confidence intervals, and account for potential design effects; transparent reporting of calculation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation with prior literature and other data
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings should be compared with previous studies (e.g., a 2014 paper showed 0% fabrication in UK biology) and interpreted in the context of existing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When results diverge markedly from existing literature, investigate methodological reasons before concluding true differences in prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caution and avoiding sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics described the findings as 'extreme' or 'click-bait' given methodological concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overstating results in press coverage or policy discussion; explicitly acknowledge limitations (sampling, method error, representativeness) and refrain from extrapolating beyond what the data support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of structural and contextual drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents and authors link questionable practices to pressures such as managerial incentives, REF-driven behaviour, and 'structural over-production.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting misconduct prevalence, consider institutional incentives and systemic causes. Policy responses should address structural drivers (evaluation systems, incentives) rather than solely individual blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: sharing instruments and data
rubrics_metrics.description: The report provides a sample questionnaire (see page 36) and a link to the full survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish survey instruments and raw (appropriately anonymised) data to allow scrutiny, replication, and re-analysis by others; this aids assessment of validity and robustness.
